label: Reliability
question: Will it stay up when something breaks?
description: Design workloads that recover automatically from failures and meet defined availability targets. Reliability encompasses resiliency (recovering from failures), availability (uptime percentage), and business continuity (data protection and disaster recovery).
keyPrinciples: Design for failure — assume every component will fail eventually
Define and validate RTO and RPO before selecting services
Use Availability Zones for intra-region redundancy
Use region pairs for cross-region disaster recovery
Automate failover — manual recovery violates RTO targets under pressure
Test recovery procedures regularly (chaos engineering)

label: Security
question: Is access controlled and data protected?
description: Protect workloads from threats through identity controls, network segmentation, data encryption, and continuous monitoring. The Zero-Trust model — verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach — underpins every security decision.
keyPrinciples: Zero-Trust: verify every access request regardless of network location
Least-privilege: assign only the permissions actually needed
Defense in depth: multiple security layers so no single control is a single point of failure
Encrypt data at rest and in transit — always
Secrets in Key Vault, never hardcoded or in environment variables
Continuous monitoring: security without observability is theater

label: Cost Optimization
question: Are we paying only for what we use?
description: Eliminate waste, right-size resources, and build financial accountability into the architecture. Cost optimization is a continuous discipline, not a one-time cleanup. FinOps — the practice of cloud financial management — requires cultural change alongside technical controls.
keyPrinciples: Measure before optimizing — 30 days of utilization data before committing to Reserved Instances
Match commitment type to workload predictability (PAYG → Savings Plan → Reserved Instance)
Storage lifecycle policies are mandatory — data accumulates silently in Hot tier
Tagging is the foundation of cost attribution — enforce at creation time via Policy
Cost awareness at design time, not post-deployment cleanup
FinOps maturity: Crawl → Walk → Run — don't prescribe Run tooling to a Crawl org

label: Operational Excellence
question: Can we deploy, monitor, and recover safely?
description: Build the processes and tooling to run workloads in production reliably over time. Operational excellence covers how changes are deployed, how the system is monitored, how incidents are detected and resolved, and how the team learns from failures.
keyPrinciples: Everything as code — infrastructure, configuration, and policy
Deploy safely with blue/green, canary, or ring deployment patterns
Observability: metrics, traces, and logs must answer 'why is this broken?' not just 'is this broken?'
Runbooks for every failure mode identified in blast radius analysis
Blameless post-incident reviews drive systemic improvement
GitOps: all changes via pull request; no manual portal changes in production

label: Performance Efficiency
question: Does it scale to meet demand without waste?
description: Match resource allocation to workload demand — scaling out when needed, scaling in when demand drops. Performance efficiency is not just about raw speed but about the architecture's ability to adapt to changing load patterns cost-effectively.
keyPrinciples: Autoscale as the default — static capacity is either over-provisioned (waste) or under-provisioned (failure)
Cache aggressively: CDN for static assets, Redis for computed aggregates, in-memory for hot data
Choose the right compute abstraction — stateless workloads on PaaS, complex orchestration on AKS
Data gravity: place compute near its primary data store to minimize egress latency and cost
Benchmark before optimizing — measure P95/P99 latency, not just averages
AI workloads have fundamentally different latency profiles (1–30s inference vs <100ms API)
